title: Spatial Autocorrelation: Global and Local Moran’s I
text:
Where we left off
Last time we turned Pennsylvania’s lung cancer cases into expected counts and SIRs. Looking at the SIR map, the eye starts to see patterns: a darker patch here, a lighter one there. Today we ask whether those patterns are real, in two steps.

Global Moran’s I — one number for the whole state: do similar SIRs tend to sit next to each other?
Local Moran’s I (LISA) — one number per county: where are the clusters and the outliers?

Between the two, we use simulation to decide what “more clustered than chance” means. Reading: Rogerson & Yamada Ch. 3–4.

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(spdep)        # neighbours, weights, Moran's I
library(SpatialEpi)   # pennLC data

theme_set(theme_classic(base_size = 12))







Note



If spdep is missing, install.packages("spdep") once.

title: Spatial Autocorrelation: Global and Local Moran’s I
text:
2.1 Queen contiguity
Two counties are neighbours if they share a border or even a single corner (like the queen in chess). poly2nb() builds the list.


Code
nb <- poly2nb(pa, queen = TRUE)
summary(card(nb))                               # neighbours per county


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  2.000   4.000   5.000   5.164   6.000   9.000 




Code
pts   <- st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(pa))
links <- nb2lines(nb, coords = pts, as_sf = TRUE) |>
  st_set_crs(st_crs(pa))

i_leh <- which(pa$county == "lehigh")
pa$role <- "other"
pa$role[nb[[i_leh]]] <- "neighbour"
pa$role[i_leh] <- "Lehigh"

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = pa, aes(fill = role), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = links, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_sf(data = pts, size = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Lehigh = "#b2182b", neighbour = "#fdae61", other = "grey90"),
                    name = NULL) +
  theme_void()








Figure 2: Queen-contiguity links between county centres. Lehigh and its neighbours are highlighted.





Other choices exist — rook contiguity (shared edges only), the k nearest centroids, or a distance band — and the answer can depend on the choice. Contiguity is the usual default for counties.

title: Spatial Autocorrelation: Global and Local Moran’s I
text:
2.2 Row-standardized weights
We turn the list into weights. With style = "W", each county’s neighbours get equal weight and the weights sum to 1, so “the neighbours’ value” is simply their average.


Code
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W")

lw$weights[[i_leh]]                             # Lehigh: equal shares


[1] 0.1666667 0.1666667 0.1666667 0.1666667 0.1666667 0.1666667

title: Spatial Autocorrelation: Global and Local Moran’s I
text:
2.3 The spatial lag
The spatial lag of a county is the average SIR of its neighbours. Mapping it next to the SIR is the most intuitive way to see autocorrelation: if the two maps look alike, neighbours resemble each other.


Code
pa$SIR_lag <- lag.listw(lw, pa$SIR)

m_own <- ggplot(pa) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cut(SIR, sir_breaks)), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  sir_fill + labs(title = "Own SIR")

m_lag <- ggplot(pa) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cut(SIR_lag, sir_breaks)), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  sir_fill + labs(title = "Neighbours' average")

(m_own | m_lag) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme_void()








Figure 3: Each county’s own SIR (left) and the average SIR of its neighbours (right).





The lag map is smoother, as averages always are. The question is whether high-SIR counties tend to have high-SIR neighbours.

title: Spatial Autocorrelation: Global and Local Moran’s I
text:
3.1 The Moran scatterplot
Plot each county’s (standardized) SIR against its neighbours’ average.


Code
pa <- pa |>
  mutate(z     = as.numeric(scale(SIR)),        # standardized SIR
         z_lag = lag.listw(lw, z))              # neighbours' average

ggplot(pa, aes(z, z_lag)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(size = E), alpha = 0.5, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#b2182b", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(data = \(x) slice_max(x, abs(z * z_lag), n = 5),
            aes(label = county), size = 3, vjust = -0.8) +
  annotate("label", x = Inf, y = Inf, label = "High-High", hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.3, colour = "#d7191c") +
  annotate("label", x = -Inf, y = -Inf, label = "Low-Low", hjust = -0.1, vjust = -0.3, colour = "#2c7bb6") +
  annotate("label", x = Inf, y = -Inf, label = "High-Low", hjust = 1.1, vjust = -0.3, colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("label", x = -Inf, y = Inf, label = "Low-High", hjust = -0.1, vjust = 1.3, colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "SIR (standardized)", y = "Neighbours' average (standardized)", size = "Expected")








Figure 4: Moran scatterplot. The slope of the line is Moran’s I.





Points in the High-High and Low-Low quadrants push the slope up (similar neighbours); points in High-Low and Low-High pull it down (dissimilar neighbours). With row-standardized weights, the slope of this line is Moran’s I.

title: Spatial Autocorrelation: Global and Local Moran’s I
text:
3.2 The statistic
\[
I = \frac{n}{\sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}} \cdot
    \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}\,(x_i-\bar x)(x_j-\bar x)}{\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^2}
\]
Read it as a correlation between each value and its neighbours’ values. Values near 0 suggest no pattern (strictly, the null expectation is \(-1/(n-1)\), about \(-0.015\) for 67 counties); positive values mean similar values cluster; negative values mean a checkerboard, which is rare for disease data.


Code
mi <- moran.test(pa$SIR, lw)

c(slope     = unname(coef(lm(z_lag ~ z, data = pa))[2]),
  Moran_I   = unname(mi$estimate[1]),
  expected  = unname(mi$estimate[2]))


      slope     Moran_I    expected 
-0.01055968 -0.01055968 -0.01515152 


The two numbers agree: Moran’s I for lung cancer SIRs is -0.011. Is that large? On its own, we cannot tell. That is what simulation is for.

title: Spatial Autocorrelation: Global and Local Moran’s I
text:
4.1 Shuffle the map
The null hypothesis says location does not matter: any county could have had any SIR. So we shuffle the 67 SIRs at random across the counties and look at the result.


Code
set.seed(374)
shuffled <- bind_rows(
  pa |> mutate(panel = "Observed"),
  pa |> mutate(SIR = sample(SIR), panel = "Shuffle 1"),
  pa |> mutate(SIR = sample(SIR), panel = "Shuffle 2"),
  pa |> mutate(SIR = sample(SIR), panel = "Shuffle 3")
)

ggplot(shuffled) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cut(SIR, sir_breaks)), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  sir_fill +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  theme_void()








Figure 5: The real SIR map (top left) and three random shufflings of the same 67 values.





Same values, same colours, different arrangement. Can you pick out the real map? If not easily, the pattern may be weak. Moran’s I turns this eyeball test into a number.

title: Spatial Autocorrelation: Global and Local Moran’s I
text:
4.2 Do it 999 times
moran.mc() shuffles the values 999 times, computes I each time, and compares the observed I with the shuffled ones.


Code
set.seed(374)
mc <- moran.mc(pa$SIR, lw, nsim = 999)
mc



    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  pa$SIR 
weights: lw  
number of simulations + 1: 1000 

statistic = -0.01056, observed rank = 552, p-value = 0.448
alternative hypothesis: greater




Code
sims <- data.frame(I = head(mc$res, -1))        # last element is the observed I

ggplot(sims, aes(I)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey75", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mc$statistic, colour = "#b2182b", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -1 / (nrow(pa) - 1), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Moran's I", y = "Number of shuffles")








Figure 6: Moran’s I under 999 random shufflings (grey) and the observed value (red).





The pseudo p-value counts how many shuffles did at least as well as the real map:
\[
p = \frac{R + 1}{999 + 1},
\]
where \(R\) is the number of shuffled I’s at or above the observed one. Here \(p =\) 0.45. With 999 shuffles, the smallest possible value is 0.001; more shuffles give finer resolution, not stronger evidence.






ImportantSIRs are not equally reliable



The shuffle treats Forest County (a handful of expected cases) and Philadelphia (over a thousand) as interchangeable. Small counties produce extreme SIRs by chance, and those extremes can create or hide apparent clustering. An Empirical Bayes version of Moran’s I (spdep::EBImoran.mc(), Assunção & Reis 1999) adjusts for this; we return to it with smoothing.

title: Spatial Autocorrelation: Global and Local Moran’s I
text:
5.1 From one number to 67
Global I says whether the map is clustered, not where. The local version gives each county its own value:
\[
I_i \propto (x_i - \bar x) \times \text{average of } (x_j - \bar x) \text{ over neighbours } j.
\]
Positive \(I_i\): the county resembles its neighbours (High-High or Low-Low). Negative \(I_i\): it differs from them (High-Low or Low-High). The local values average to the global I — each county’s share of the overall pattern.

title: Spatial Autocorrelation: Global and Local Moran’s I
text:
5.2 Conditional permutation
Significance is again simulated, with one twist: county \(i\) is held fixed and only the other values are shuffled around it. This asks whether \(i\)’s particular neighbourhood is unusual, given \(i\)’s own value.


Code
set.seed(374)
lisa <- localmoran_perm(pa$SIR, lw, nsim = 999)

pa <- pa |>
  mutate(
    Ii    = lisa[, "Ii"],
    p_sim = lisa[, "Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim"],                     # simulation-based p
    quad  = as.character(attr(lisa, "quadr")$mean)            # scatterplot quadrant
  )

c(mean_local = mean(pa$Ii), global = unname(mi$estimate[1]))  # same number


 mean_local      global 
-0.01055968 -0.01055968 




Code
m_Ii <- ggplot(pa) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = Ii), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey95", high = "#b2182b", name = "Local I") +
  labs(title = "Local I")

m_p <- ggplot(pa) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cut(p_sim, c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 1))), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#7f0000", "#d7301f", "#fdbb84", "grey95"),
                    labels = c("< 0.01", "0.01--0.05", "0.05--0.10", "> 0.10"),
                    drop = FALSE, name = "p") +
  labs(title = "Significance")

(m_Ii | m_p) & theme_void()








Figure 7: Local Moran’s I (left) and its simulated p-value (right).

title: Spatial Autocorrelation: Global and Local Moran’s I
text:
5.3 The LISA cluster map
Combining the two maps — quadrant for significant counties, grey otherwise — gives the classic LISA map.


Code
lisa_cols <- c("High-High" = "#d7191c", "Low-Low" = "#2c7bb6",
               "High-Low"  = "#fdae61", "Low-High" = "#abd9e9",
               "Not significant" = "grey92")

pa <- pa |>
  mutate(cluster = factor(if_else(p_sim < 0.05, quad, "Not significant"),
                          levels = names(lisa_cols)))

m_lisa <- ggplot(pa) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cluster), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = lisa_cols, drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "LISA clusters")

(m_own | m_lisa) & theme_void()








Figure 8: SIR (left) and LISA clusters at p < 0.05 (right).







Code
pa |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(cluster != "Not significant") |>
  arrange(cluster, p_sim) |>
  transmute(county, cluster, O, E = round(E, 1), SIR = round(SIR, 2),
            Ii = round(Ii, 2), p_sim)

High-High (hot spot): high SIR, high-SIR neighbours.
Low-Low (cold spot): low SIR, low-SIR neighbours.
High-Low / Low-High (spatial outliers): a county that breaks from its surroundings.

A High-High county is the centre of a cluster; its neighbours belong to the cluster but need not be significant themselves.

title: Spatial Autocorrelation: Global and Local Moran’s I
section: 5.4 How much should we believe it?
text:
5.4 How much should we believe it?


Code
m_strict <- pa |>
  mutate(cluster = factor(if_else(p_sim < 0.01, quad, "Not significant"),
                          levels = names(lisa_cols))) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cluster), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = lisa_cols, drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "p < 0.01")

(m_lisa + labs(title = "p < 0.05") | m_strict) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme_void()








Figure 9: LISA clusters at p < 0.05 (left) and p < 0.01 (right).











Warning67 tests, not one



At \(p < 0.05\), about \(0.05 \times 67 \approx 3\) counties would be flagged even if lung cancer risk had no spatial structure at all. Neighbouring tests also share data, so they are not independent. Treat LISA output as a map of places worth a closer look, not as a list of confirmed clusters. Clusters that survive a stricter threshold, involve counties with large \(E_i\), and make epidemiological sense deserve the most attention.
